results.content: # Bayesian State-Space Model Ultimate Guide. * Introduction to State-Space Models. ## Introduction to State-Space Models. State-space models provide a mathematical framework to represent dynamic systems by modeling latent processes (states) which evolve over time and are indirectly observed through noisy measurements. A state-space model decomposes a system into:. A conventional state-space model is defined by two main equations:. flowchart TD A["Previous State $$ x_{t-1} $$"] --> B["Transition Model $$ f( \cdot ) $$"] B --> C["Current State $$ x_t $$"] C --> D["Observation Model $$ g( \cdot ) $$"] D --> E["Observation $$ y_t $$"] subgraph Noise Effects F["Process Noise $$ \epsilon_t $$"] --> B G["Measurement Noise $$ \eta_t $$"] --> D end. The diagram above captures the recursive nature of state evolution and observation generation, a central idea in state-space modeling. In Bayesian state-space modelling, uncertainty is addressed using the principles of Bayesian inference. Rather than relying solely on point estimates, Bayesian methods quantify uncertainty by calculating probability distributions over the states and parameters of the model. According to Bayes' theorem, for a parameter $$ \theta $$ (which could be a latent state, a model parameter, etc.) given data $$ D $$, the relationship is formulated as:. The likelihood function is a core component that relates the observed data to the latent states and parameters of the model. In the context of the state-space model, the likelihood incorporates both the transition and observation models. For example, for a simple linear Gaussian state-space model, the likelihood takes the form:. Several algorithms have been developed to perform inference in state-space models, with each suited to different types of systems and noise characteristics. For nonlinear state-space models or those with non-Gaussian noise, the Kalman filter may no longer be optimal. A critical step in Bayesian state-space modeling is the estimation of parameters. Selecting the appropriate state-space model and its complexity is crucial. Bayesian state-space models are not only theoretically appealing but also highly practical. Libraries such as PyMC, NumPy, and SciPy provide efficient tools for building and sampling from Bayesian state-space models. Title: State Space Models
# State Space Models. + Components of state space models. ## State Space Models. * Distributions \(\{f\_t(),g\_t()\}\_{t=1}^{T}\) (and sometimes initial state \(x\_0\)) are parameters of model. + Also get sequence of filtered distributions \(p(x\_{t}|\mathcal{Y}\_{t})\) which give best guess of state as of time \(t\). ## Linear State Space Model. ## Multivariate Linear State Space Model. + Any ARIMA model has a state space representation. * Observation equation is \(y\_t=x\_{1,t}\): 0 coefficient on all states except current. ## Estimation of Linear State Space Models. * If observation and state equation *known*, filter produces conditional likelihood \(\ell(y\_{t+1}|\mathcal{Y}\_T)\) to use for forecasting. * Exponential smoothing models are particularly simple class of state space models. + Unlike generic state space models, because only one shock, can recover components exactly rather than perform smoothing. * Based on this, build less restricted linear state space model and apply Bayesian estimate using BSTS. library(fredr) #FRED Data library(fpp2) # Forecasting tools library(bsts) #Bayesian State Space Models library(gridExtra) #Graph Display fredr_set_key("8782f247febb41f291821950cf9118b6") #Key I obtained for this class #One Year Percent Change in Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers INFLATION<-fredr(series_id = "CPIAUCSL",units="pc1",vintage_dates = as.Date("2021-04-08")) #Fed Funds Rate FEDFUNDS<-fredr(series_id = "FEDFUNDS",vintage_dates = as.Date("2021-04-08")) fedfunds<-ts(FEDFUNDS$value,frequency=12,start=c(1954,7),end=c(2021,2),names="FFR") inflation1<-ts(INFLATION$value,frequency=12,start=c(1947,1),end=c(2021,2),names="CPI") #Truncate to same window as Fed Funds Rate inflation<-window(inflation1,start=c(1954,7)) #monetarydata<-as.ts(data.frame(inflation,fedfunds),frequency=12,start=c(1954,7)) # Estimate Exponential Smoothing Model of Inflation # Choose components by AICc, estimate parameters by maximum likelihood inflETSmodel<-ets(inflation) #Construct 6 month forecast inflETSfcst<-forecast(inflETSmodel,h=6). # Build a Bayesian State Space Model of Inflation #Start by adding components to specification object ss<-AddSemilocalLinearTrend( state.specification = list(), #Initialize with empty list y=inflation) #Use data to define scale of prior ss<-AddDynamicRegression(state.specification=ss, inflation~fedfunds) # Set number of MCMC draws, and number to discard as "burn in" in analysis niter<-1000 burnins<-500 #Construct model posterior by MCMC sampling model <- bsts(inflation, state.specification = ss, niter = niter). #Time series of posterior distributions for trend and dynamic regression components PlotBstsComponents(model). * State space models with Bayesian priors over equations provide reasonable forecast performance. + Comes from multivariate state space model with many components corresponding to macroeconomic relationships. * State Space Models are structured way to build model from many probabilistic and deterministic components. * Case studies of state space models for forecasting with BSTS library.

results.title: Mastering MCMC for Bayesian Analysis
results.content:
Title: Mastering MCMC for Bayesian Analysis
At its core lies Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), a set of algorithms that sample from complex posterior distributions when analytical solutions are intractable. This article, "Mastering MCMC for Bayesian Analysis", explores the nuances of MCMC methods, detailing algorithm selection, parameter tuning, convergence diagnostics, and implementation practices. MH is the archetypal MCMC method where a candidate sample is drawn from a proposal distribution, and then accepted or rejected based on a ratio involving the target posterior density. During the initial iterations, the algorithm adjusts the step size to ensure that the sampling efficiently traverses the high-probability regions of the posterior. High autocorrelation indicates that the chain is not exploring the parameter space effectively, reducing the effective sample size. data { int N; // number of observations vector[N] x; // predictor variable vector[N] y; // response variable } parameters { real alpha; // intercept real beta; // slope real sigma; // noise standard deviation } model { // Priors alpha ~ normal(0, 10); beta ~ normal(0, 10); sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5); // Likelihood y ~ normal(alpha + beta * x, sigma); } This simple model demonstrates how Stan facilitates Bayesian inference by compiling the model and enabling efficient sampling via HMC/NUTS. Below is an example of a Bayesian linear regression model in PyMC3: ```python import pymc3 as pm import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt np.random.seed(42) N = 100 x = np.linspace(0, 10, N) alpha_true = 2.0 beta_true = 0.5 sigma_true = 1.0 y = alpha_true + beta_true * x + np.random.normal(0, sigma_true, N) with pm.Model() as model: # Priors for unknown parameters alpha = pm.Normal('alpha', mu=0, sigma=10) beta = pm.Normal('beta', mu=0, sigma=10) sigma = pm.HalfCauchy('sigma', beta=5) # Likelihood (sampling distribution) of observations mu = alpha + beta * x y_obs = pm.Normal('y_obs', mu=mu, sigma=sigma, observed=y) # Inference trace = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, target_accept=0.8) pm.traceplot(trace) plt.show() This code snippet outlines a straightforward approach to implementing Bayesian linear regression using PyMC3. ### Burn-in and Thinning Strategies - **Burn-in Period:** The burn-in period involves discarding an initial set of samples to allow the chain to converge to the target distribution. Practical implementations in Stan and PyMC3 not only simplify the modeling process but also embed best practices such as burn-in, thinning, and effective sample size estimation right into the analytical workflow.

results.content: # MCMC, Monte Carlo likelihood estimation, and the bootstrap particle filter. In a previous post I described a generalisation of the Metropolis Hastings MCMC algorithm which uses unbiased Monte Carlo estimates of likelihood in the acceptance ratio, but is nevertheless exact, when considered as a pseudo-marginal approach to “exact approximate” MCMC. To be useful in the context of Bayesian inference, we need to be able to compute unbiased estimates of the (marginal) likelihood of the data given some proposed model parameters with any “latent variables” integrated out. This simple Monte Carlo estimate of likelihood can therefore be substituted into a Metropolis-Hastings acceptance ratio without affecting the (marginal) target distribution of the Markov chain. It is clear from our understanding of importance resampling that these weights are appropriate for representing a sample from , and so the particles and weights can be propagated forward to the next time point. It is also clear that the average weight at each time gives an estimate of the marginal likelihood of the current data point given the data so far. It should therefore be clear that if one is interested in developing MCMC algorithms for state space models, one can use a pseudo-marginal MCMC scheme, substituting in from a bootstrap particle filter in place of . ## 12 thoughts on “MCMC, Monte Carlo likelihood estimation, and the bootstrap particle filter”. 1.
